extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials and rulemaking staff; administrative law policymakers and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how administrative agencies should detect, manage, evaluate, and augment public comments (including mass, malattributed, and computer-generated submissions) in notice-and-comment rulemaking. Covers technological tools (NLP, de-duplication, summarization), participatory innovations (prize challenges, mini-publics, collaborative annotation), and policy/ethical/legal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over source
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is the substance of comments that matters, as opposed to the identity of submitters or the volume of comments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude or disregard comments merely because they are computer-generated or part of a mass campaign; instead, consider whether a comment raises significant issues requiring agency consideration. Agencies should focus on identifying and responding to substantive issues regardless of commenter identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-duplication as mass comment management
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies extensively use de-duplication software to help them process mass comment campaigns; with de-duplication software, the unique content in computer-generated comments can be readily identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat management of computer-generated and mass comments primarily as a de-duplication task: use de-duplication to surface unique substantive content and reduce volume-based burden on reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor evolving technology threats
rubrics_metrics.description: “it will be important to monitor whether the technologies that enable mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments threaten to undermine the perceived legitimacy of the notice-and-comment process and the ability of agency officials to make sense of and consider comments thoughtfully.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously assess whether advances (e.g., AI that closely mimics human content) render detection/prevention impractical and whether those advances could undermine legitimacy; adjust detection and policy responses over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and publicize comment policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop and publicize policies that will encourage helpful comments and discourage or prohibit misleading ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear, public-facing policies describing desired comment attributes and disallowed practices; use these policies as the first, modest mechanism to deter abuse rather than relying on criminal enforcement or blanket prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available software tools to screen, sort, and summarize
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should take advantage of the many software tools that are increasingly available to screen, sort, de-duplicate, summarize, and digest submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy NLP and computational tools (e.g., de-duping, topic modeling, automated summarization, sentiment analysis, plagiarism detection, readability metrics, word embeddings) to extract relevant substantive information, spot patterns, and prioritize comments for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: NLP techniques and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) includes tools such as Flesch-Kincaid Readability, LIWC, plagiarism detection, automated document summarization, sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and word embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specific techniques where appropriate: readability metrics to gauge clarity, LIWC for psychological/linguistic patterns, plagiarism detection for similarity, topic modeling for semantic sorting, summarization to condense content, and embeddings for semantic searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine automation with human oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes combine automation with human intelligence to make quick work of large data stores and overcome the biases that arise from using automation alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human review to validate and correct machine outputs; example: the State Department provided a public opportunity to review machine-generated summaries and credited the combination of human and machine intelligence for efficiency and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public review/ accountability for machine summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department used a third-party software company to create summaries and later gave the public an opportunity to review the summaries, 'adding accountability but in a way that is efficient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deploying automated summarization, provide transparent processes (e.g., public review of summaries) and human checks to ensure summaries reliably reflect underlying comments and to preserve public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrain models for domain-specific language
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the challenges for deploying summarizing technology in the context of rulemaking is that there is often domain specific language that requires retraining the relevant models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in retraining and domain adaptation of NLP models for rulemakings with specialized vocabulary; where large comment volumes are expected, such investment may be worthwhile to improve tool performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider legal obligations and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency staff expressed concerns related to how the use of new technologies might interact with their legal obligation to review and respond to comments. This legal uncertainty creates the risk that agencies may innovate slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deploying automated tools, evaluate legal risks and compliance obligations (e.g., requirements to consider comments); design workflows that ensure tools support, rather than supplant, legally mandated review duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology to augment, not replace, human review
rubrics_metrics.description: While NLP tools can be used to augment, rather than replace, human review, agency staff expressed concerns related to how the use of new technologies might interact with their legal obligation to review and respond to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat automated outputs as triage or synthesis aids; retain human decisionmakers in the loop for substantive interpretation, legal assessment, and final determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize-backed challenges with explicit evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize-backed challenges require agencies to articulate and define exactly what information they need from the public and provide very transparent and specific criteria for evaluating public submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Challenge.gov-style prize competitions when the regulatory problem benefits from innovation: define clear problem statements and transparent evaluation criteria to attract and fairly assess submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sourcing and crowdsourced expert advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert sourcing, where officials crowdsource expert advice, is one example of how government bodies are implementing more citizen engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowdsource expert input (e.g., drafting questions, running deliberative sessions) to supplement internal expertise; use videoconferencing and online coordination to convene experts efficiently for policy-relevant input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative annotation platforms for draft rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Online collaborative annotation makes it possible to hear from a broader and deeper range of experts; the German government used an annotation platform (Hypothes.is) to solicit input on its draft AI policy, enabling people to see one another’s feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use annotation platforms to solicit targeted, visible expert comments on draft texts, enabling interactive commentary and deeper, document-focused engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative mini-publics and citizen juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments are experimenting with the use of random samples of members of the public (mini-publics, citizen juries, citizen assemblies) as mechanisms to obtain more legitimate forms of participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use randomly selected, demographically representative panels to elicit deliberative input and oversight; provide background materials and deliberative polling to inform participants and produce considered recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selected participation tools (Evidence Checks, wiki surveys)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-selected participation mechanisms like UK parliament Evidence Checks and 'wiki surveys' (All Our Ideas) allow experts, stakeholders, and the public to comment or choose between paired options; wiki surveys show two options and allow participants to pick or submit alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy self-selected, platform-based exercises to quickly gather informed input or validate evidence; wiki surveys can be more efficient than open-ended commenting for eliciting preferences and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate among types of problematic comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comments pose management challenges but do not threaten the legitimacy of the process; malattributed comments pose a threat (albeit a small one) of harm to third parties; computer-generated comments are not problematic per se but may pose issues if they are misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor agency responses to the type of pathology: use management tools for mass campaigns, investigate malattribution when third-party harm is plausible, and evaluate computer-generated content for misleading substantive claims rather than excluding it automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer technological and policy responses over criminal enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal objection to the public’s ability to submit mass comments... The solution here is likely not criminal prosecution... Agencies should respond ... in two more modest ways. First, develop and publicize policies... Second, the response to abuses of new technologies rests on more technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reflexive referrals to DOJ or sweeping bans; prioritize policy clarity and deployment of technical tools (screening, de-duplication, summarization) to manage and mitigate abuses while preserving participation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance broadened participation with agency resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Public participation should 'neither frustrate an agency’s control of the allocation of its resources nor unduly complicate and delay its proceedings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing participation processes or adopting new engagement tools, account for agency capacity and resource allocation to prevent undue complication or delay in rulemaking.
